title: JavaScript
subtitle: Deep Dive
description: From execution contexts to memory management — understand JavaScript the way the engine does.
longDescription: Most developers learn JavaScript by copying patterns. This phase goes inside the engine — execution contexts, closures, prototypes, the event loop — so you understand WHY things work, not just how to use them.

concepts.title: Execution Context & Call Stack
concepts.tldr: Every time JavaScript runs code, it creates an execution context — a container holding variables, scope, and the 'this' value. The call stack tracks which context is currently running.
concepts.problem: You've seen 'undefined' where you expected a value, or 'ReferenceError: Cannot access X before initialization' and had no idea why. You've written code that works in one order but breaks in another. These bugs come from not understanding when JavaScript reads your code vs when it runs it.
concepts.analogy: Imagine a chef (JavaScript engine) with a notepad. Before cooking anything, the chef scans the entire recipe and writes down all ingredient names (variables) but leaves blanks for their values. Only then does the chef start actually cooking (executing). That scan phase is 'hoisting.' The notepad is the execution context.
concepts.deep:
JavaScript creates two types of execution contexts: the Global Execution Context (GEC) created once when the script loads, and Function Execution Contexts created every time a function is called.

Each context has two phases:
1. CREATION PHASE: JS scans the code. var declarations are hoisted to undefined. Function declarations are hoisted fully (name + body). let/const are hoisted but placed in the Temporal Dead Zone — they exist but cannot be accessed.
2. EXECUTION PHASE: Code runs line by line. Variables get assigned their actual values.

The SCOPE CHAIN is built during creation: each context holds a reference to its outer environment. When a variable lookup fails in the current context, JS walks up the chain until it reaches the global context.

The CALL STACK is a LIFO data structure. Each function call pushes a new execution context frame. When the function returns, the frame pops. Maximum stack depth is engine-dependent (~10,000–15,000 in V8).
concepts.summary: Every JavaScript program runs inside execution contexts. Understanding the two-phase lifecycle (create → execute) explains hoisting, TDZ, and scope chains — the source of most 'mysterious' JS bugs.

concepts.title: Closures
concepts.tldr: A closure is a function that remembers the variables from its birth environment even after that environment is gone. It's not magic — it's memory.
concepts.problem: You've hit the classic loop bug where all setTimeout callbacks print the same number. You've tried to make 'private' variables in JavaScript and failed. You don't understand why React's useState works the way it does. All of these are closure problems.
concepts.analogy: When you leave home for college, you carry a backpack with things from home — your mom's recipes, your dad's advice. The 'home' might change, but your backpack (closure) keeps those references. The function is you; the backpack is the closed-over variables; home is the outer scope.
concepts.summary: Closures give functions persistent memory. Master them and you understand debounce, throttle, memoize, the module pattern, React hooks, and 90% of functional programming patterns.
